sections.title: LLMs from Spring Boot

blocks.title: Not from your PDFs
blocks.text: No guide of yours covers this, so this page was written for the site, as of October 2026. Tools and versions change quickly: check the official documentation before relying on details.

blocks: Spring AI gives you a portable API over model providers, in normal Spring style. LangChain4j is the main alternative, and the concepts are the same. The examples here follow the Spring AI 2.0 documentation.

blocks.title: pom.xml, with the Spring AI BOM managing the version
The key comes from the environment, never from Git
Provider property names
blocks.text: Model names and properties change often. Take current values from the Spring AI and provider documentation.

blocks.title: A real feature in 20 lines

walkthrough.title: A record as schema
walkthrough.text: The output is mapped to a Java record, so the rest of your code stays typed.

walkthrough.title: Builder injection
walkthrough.text: Spring Boot auto-configures `ChatClient.Builder`. The system prompt holds your instructions.

walkthrough.title: The call
walkthrough.text: `entity` converts the response. The model is called at this point, so it needs a timeout and error handling.

blocks.title: Validate the result
blocks.text: A typed result can still be wrong. Validate it (for example, priority within 1 to 3) before acting on it.

blocks.title: The user sees text at once rather than waiting

sections.title: Treat it like any remote dependency

rows: Set explicitly; retry only rate limits and transient errors
Log token usage per feature and user, and rate-limit users
Degrade gracefully: the app should work when the model is down
Mock `ChatModel` in unit tests; use evaluations for quality
Know what data you send to the provider, and remove what isn't needed

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
- `ChatClient` is the entry point.
- `entity()` maps output to records, but validate the values.
- Stream for user-facing text.
- Add timeouts, limits and fallbacks as for any remote call.

items.question: Why inject `ChatClient.Builder` rather than hard-coding a provider?
items.answer: Configuration chooses the model, so you can switch providers, and tests can substitute it.

items.question: When is `.call()` actually sent to the model?
items.answer: When a terminal method such as `content()`, `entity()` or `chatResponse()` runs.
